transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 56 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Rachel Kim (Orchid CTO), Sanjay Rao (Infra), Elena Torres (SRE), Tom Nguyen (Data Scientist)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to validate observability plan for a pilot: they want token-level visibility, prefix/KV cache prefetch heatmaps, and end-to-end OTEL integration feeding Grafana dashboards. Main concerns: noise & high-cardinality, network egress for VPC deployment, quantization regressions affecting latency vs quality.

Topics: OTEL spans for tokens, KV cache prefetch heuristics, batching effects on latency P50/P95, quantization profiles impact on perf, VPC/on-prem telemetry routing, sample dashboard layout (heatmaps + span flamegraphs).

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros then we'll jump into the telemetry ask from Orchid. Liam and I are from Redwood; we'll mostly keep it technical.
[00:00:18] Rachel Kim: Hi, Rachel here. We're trying to instrument our inference pipeline for better debugging — specifically token-level patterns and see when the KV cache helps or hurts.
[00:00:28] Liam O'Connor: Cool, yeah. To set expectations, token-level traces are doable with OpenTelemetry but we need to be careful about cardinality — you don't want a span per token indiscriminately.
[00:00:40] Sanjay Rao: Agreed. Our concern is storage and egress if we're on a VPC/private deployment. We can't ship terabytes of token spans to SaaS.
[00:00:48] Liam O'Connor: Right. Typical approach is selective sampling + aggregated metrics. We emit a small set of high-cardinality attributes at span creation (model_version, route, request_id, token_index for sampled traces) and then roll up per-route token-latency histograms.
[00:01:05] Elena Torres: Can you explain what you mean by "token_index for sampled traces"? Sounds like we might still be logging every position.
[00:01:12] Liam O'Connor: Good point. We only include token_index inside spans for sampled requests — e.g., 1% of requests or a targeted sampling of slow requests or errors. For the rest, we emit counters and histograms keyed by token_bucket (e.g., first-32, 33-128, >128) so you can build heatmaps without huge cardinality.
[00:01:31] Tom Nguyen: Heatmaps are exactly what we need — like prefetch hit-rate by token position and time-of-day. Do you have an example visualization?
[00:01:39] Maya Patel: We'll attach a sample Grafana dashboard after the call. It shows a 2D heatmap: x-axis token position, y-axis hour-of-day, color is prefetch hit-rate or latency delta when prefetching on vs off.
[00:01:52] Rachel Kim: Nice. Our other question is around prefetch heuristics — Redwood mentions preemptive KV prefetching. How aggressive should we be?
[00:02:00] Liam O'Connor: It's workload dependent. For chat-style with short turns, prefetching the next 32 tokens is low risk. For long-form generation, you want adaptive windows — score prefixes by reuse probability and prefetch only if expected value exceeds the memory/cost tradeoff.
[00:02:16] Sanjay Rao: Memory is a hard limit for us. If we prefetch too much on dedicated GPUs we blow memory and start swapping. How does Redwood indicate memory pressure?
[00:02:25] Liam O'Connor: The runtime exports GPU memory usage metrics and per-model KV cache size. We can correlate those with OTEL resource metrics and add a high-water mark alert. Also the runtime supports eviction strategies (LRU, TTL-based, size-based) that can be toggled.
[00:02:38] Elena Torres: On VPC/private, will the OTEL collector run inside our VPC? We don't want outbound ports opened.
[00:02:45] Maya Patel: Yes — for Private you can run a local OTEL collector that ships to your telemetry backend. Redwood's control plane can accept compressed batched spans over TLS through a customer-controlled egress endpoint, or you can keep everything in your network and point Grafana at the local Prometheus/OTLP endpoint.
[00:02:58] Rachel Kim: We run an on-prem Grafana + Tempo for traces. Can Redwood push spans to Tempo directly?
[00:03:05] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely. We can configure OTLP/HTTP exporter to point at your Tempo. We typically provide an example collector config that enriches spans with model metadata and masks PII.
[00:03:14] Tom Nguyen: How do you structure spans? Do you do a single span per request with attributes for token timings or many child spans per token?
[00:03:21] Liam O'Connor: We usually do a hybrid: a parent span per request, with aggregated attributes and timing. For sampled traces we add child spans for key lifecycle events: model_load, kv_prefetch, kv_lookup, kernel_exec. For per-token granularity we add lightweight sub-spans or events but only on sampled traffic to avoid explosion.
[00:03:40] Rachel Kim: And token-level metrics for dashboards — is that derived from spans or emitted as metrics?
[00:03:45] Liam O'Connor: Derived. We emit OTEL metrics (histograms/counters) for token_latency_buckets and prefetch_hit_counters. Spans provide context and flamegraphs for debugging. Metrics feed the heatmaps.
[00:03:55] Sanjay Rao: Ok. What about quantization? We expect to try 4-bit quantized models to save memory. Any telemetry blind spots there?
[00:04:03] Liam O'Connor: Quantization changes step latency and quality. We recommend tagging spans with quant_profile (e.g., int4-gptq, q8) so you can slice by profile. Important: 4-bit can reduce memory but sometimes increases kernel overhead due to dequant/decompress; our kernel selector logs kernel_variant which you can correlate to spikes in p99.
[00:04:20] Tom Nguyen: If we see a quality regression, can we do A/B on model variants with telemetry?
[00:04:24] Maya Patel: Yes — Redwood's rollout supports canary/A-B and our SDK emits variant_id. Combine that with output-quality evals (we can optionally run automated prompt evals) and the token-level traces to detect regressions.
[00:04:35] Elena Torres: Back to prefetch: can we get a heatmap that shows latency when prefetch hits vs misses, and the number of tokens that were prefetched?
[00:04:43] Liam O'Connor: Yes. Example metric: prefetch_latency_delta_seconds{bucket="1-32"} and prefetch_hit_rate{bucket="1-32"}. Then a Grafana heatmap layer compares the delta per bucket by time. We'll include the example.
[00:04:56] Rachel Kim: A practical point — sampling. We want fidelity for error troubleshooting but not the volume. What's a recommended sampling configuration?
[00:05:03] Liam O'Connor: Start with 0.5-1% global sampling, plus tail-based sampling for requests that exceed a P95 latency threshold or return an error code. Also sample all requests from a small list of customer IDs during pilot. Tail-based sampling yields high signal for issues without the noise.
[00:05:18] Sanjay Rao: How intrusive is the instrumentation? Will adding spans add CPU overhead on the host?
[00:05:23] Liam O'Connor: Minimal for aggregated metrics. Per-span instrumentation does add some overhead—roughly low single-digit percent on CPU if you're creating many spans per token, which is why sampling is recommended. The runtime does lightweight counters in the hot path and offloads detailed span creation to a background worker where possible.
[00:05:38] Tom Nguyen: For our pilot, we want to run a synthetic workload with bursts and see cache warmup behavior. Can Redwood simulate that or should we provide traces?
[00:05:46] Maya Patel: We can provide a load script that mimics your traffic shape (turn lengths, concurrency) and attach it to the pilot cluster. But we need representative traces to tune prefetch heuristics — Rachel, can you share a week of anonymized request profiles?
[00:05:58] Rachel Kim: Yes I'll extract and scrub them, aim to get that by Friday.
[00:06:03] Liam O'Connor: Great. On the dashboard side, we'll include: 1) Prefetch hit-rate heatmap, 2) Token-latency P50/P95 by bucket, 3) Kernel variant flamegraph (showing heavy kernels), 4) Memory pressure timeline with eviction events.
[00:06:18] Elena Torres: Any red flags we should watch for when moving to private deployment?
[00:06:22] Liam O'Connor: Network latency to model shards if you're multi-zone, egress rules for the OTEL collector, KMS/HSM configurations for keys — those are the usual items. We'll share a network diagram template.
[00:06:33] Maya Patel: Also, SLA differences: Dedicated/private options have different latency SLOs. We'll call that out in the pilot proposal.
[00:06:40] Rachel Kim: One last thing — audit logs. We need to ensure token traces don't contain PII. How do you handle masking?
[00:06:46] Liam O'Connor: We have sanitizer hooks in the collector config. You can define masking rules (regex, token-level redaction) and we also support deterministic hashing of identifiers so you can correlate without exposing PII.
[00:06:58] Tom Nguyen: OK, that helps.
[00:07:00] Maya Patel: Cool — I'll recap next steps. We'll attach the example Grafana dashboard, OTEL collector snippet, and the pilot proposal. Liam will produce the collector config and example spans. Rachel will share the traces. We'll reconvene after pilot start.
[00:07:12] Rachel Kim: Thanks, this was helpful.

Recap / Notes:
- Agreed telemetry pattern: aggregated metrics + selective per-token sampled spans.
- Heatmaps built from token buckets to avoid cardinality explosion.
- Prefetch heuristics: adaptive, start small (next-32), test widening windows on high-reuse workloads.
- Quantization: tag spans with quant_profile; watch kernel_variant spikes for perf regressions.
- Private deployment: run OTEL collector inside VPC, route to local Tempo/Grafana or allow compressed batched egress to customer endpoint.

Explicit next steps (as above):
1) Liam to provide OTEL config + example spans by 2026-04-05.
2) Rachel to supply anonymized 7-day trace sample by 2026-04-02.
